blocks.text: The p-value is the single number that hypothesis testing collapses an entire experiment down to, and it is also the most consistently misunderstood number in applied statistics. It measures how surprising the observed data would be if the null hypothesis were true, nothing more, yet it is routinely misread as the probability that a hypothesis is true or the probability of having made a mistake. Understanding precisely what a p-value is, and just as importantly what it is not, is essential for anyone reading an A/B test dashboard or a model comparison report.

blocks.alt: How a p-value is produced and used
blocks.caption: From an assumed null hypothesis to a reject or fail to reject decision

blocks.text: 1. Formal Definition

The p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually measured, calculated under the assumption that the null hypothesis H0 is true. It is a conditional probability: it describes how likely the data is, given the null hypothesis, not how likely the null hypothesis is, given the data.

"At least as extreme" is defined relative to the direction of the alternative hypothesis. For a two-tailed test, it includes results as far from the null value in either direction. For a one-tailed test, it includes only results at least as far in the one direction specified by the alternative hypothesis. This is why the same raw test statistic can produce two different p-values depending on how the test was set up before the data was collected.

blocks.title: In plain language
blocks.content: A p-value of 0.03 means: if there really were no effect, a result this extreme, or more extreme, would happen about 3 percent of the time by chance alone.

blocks.text: The phrase at least as extreme is doing important work in that definition, it accounts for results even more surprising than what was observed, not just the exact observed value, which is why the p-value calculation looks at an entire tail of a distribution rather than a single point.

This definition ties directly back to the hypothesis testing lesson, the p-value is the piece of evidence that gets compared against the significance level alpha to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis.
2. The Direct Connection to Alpha

The p-value only becomes a decision once it is compared against the significance level alpha chosen before the experiment, as covered in the hypothesis testing lesson. The rule is mechanical: if the p-value is less than alpha, reject the null hypothesis; if the p-value is greater than or equal to alpha, fail to reject it.

With the conventional alpha equals 0.05, a p-value of 0.04 clears the bar and counts as statistically significant, while a p-value of 0.06 does not, even though the two numbers are barely different. This sharp cutoff around an arbitrary round number is itself a frequent source of confusion, since a result just above the threshold is not meaningfully weaker evidence than a result just below it.

code.content:
from scipy import stats

t_statistic, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(treatment_sample, control_sample)
alpha = 0.05

if p_value < alpha:
    print(f"p-value {p_value:.4f} < alpha {alpha}: reject H0")
else:
    print(f"p-value {p_value:.4f} >= alpha {alpha}: fail to reject H0")

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: With alpha set at 0.05, a computed p-value of 0.03 falls below the threshold, leading to a reject the null decision, while a p-value of 0.08 falls above it, leading to a fail to reject decision, even though 0.03 and 0.08 are not dramatically different numbers.

blocks.text: Alpha is chosen before running the test, exactly as the hypothesis testing lesson describes, choosing it after seeing the p-value defeats the entire purpose of setting a threshold in advance.
3. The Single Most Common Misinterpretation

A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. This is the single most common and most consequential misreading of the entire concept, and it appears constantly in casual reporting, dashboards, and even some published research. The p-value is computed by assuming H0 is true from the start, so it cannot simultaneously be a statement about the probability that H0 is true; that would be circular.

A p-value of 0.03 does not mean there is a 3 percent chance the null hypothesis is correct, nor does it mean there is a 97 percent chance the alternative hypothesis is correct. The probability that a fixed hypothesis is "true" is not something a single p-value can measure at all under the standard framework it comes from; that kind of statement belongs to a different branch of statistics, Bayesian inference, which starts from prior probabilities rather than a fixed null assumption.

This is worth restating plainly since it is so consistently misunderstood: a p-value of 0.03 does not mean there is a 97 percent chance the alternative hypothesis is true, it means that, assuming the null hypothesis were true, data this extreme would occur about 3 percent of the time.
3.1 It Is Also Not the Probability of Making a Mistake

A second closely related error is treating the p-value as the probability that rejecting H0 would be a mistake, that is, the chance of a Type I error for this specific decision. That is also wrong. Alpha, the pre-chosen threshold, is the long-run Type I error rate of the testing procedure across repeated experiments; the p-value is a property of this one dataset, and confusing the two conflates a long-run frequency with a single-instance probability.
3.2 What the P-Value Actually Tells You

Stripped down to its precise meaning, the p-value answers exactly one question: "assuming nothing interesting is going on, how often would data like this, or more extreme, show up just from sampling noise?" A small p-value says the observed data would be a rare coincidence under that assumption, which is evidence, not proof, against the assumption.

blocks.text: 4. P-Hacking and the Multiple Comparisons Problem

P-hacking refers to any practice that searches through data or analysis choices until a p-value below alpha is found, then reports only that result. Common forms include testing many outcome metrics until one happens to be significant, repeatedly peeking at results and stopping the experiment the moment significance appears, or trying several different statistical tests and reporting whichever gives the smallest p-value.

The underlying mathematics is simple: at alpha equals 0.05, a true null hypothesis has a 5 percent chance of producing a false positive on any single test, purely by chance. Run twenty independent tests on data with no real effect anywhere, and the expected number of false positives is one, purely from chance, even though every single test looks individually legitimate.

P-hacking describes any practice, deliberate or accidental, of trying many different analyses, subgroups, or stopping points until a significant p-value happens to appear, then reporting only that result as if it were the single planned test.

Preregistering an analysis plan before collecting data, stating exactly which test will be run and how, is one of the most effective defenses against accidentally p-hacking a result without realizing it.
4.1 The Multiple Comparisons Problem

This is called the multiple comparisons problem: as the number of tests run against the same data grows, the probability that at least one produces a false positive grows rapidly, even if alpha for each individual test stays at 0.05. With 20 independent tests, the chance of at least one false positive is roughly 1 minus 0.95 raised to the 20th power, which works out to about 64 percent, far higher than the 5 percent an unwary reader might assume.

code.content:
# Probability of at least one false positive across n independent
# tests, each with significance level alpha, when H0 is true everywhere
def chance_of_at_least_one_false_positive(alpha, n_tests):
    return 1 - (1 - alpha) ** n_tests

print(chance_of_at_least_one_false_positive(0.05, 1))   # 0.05
print(chance_of_at_least_one_false_positive(0.05, 20))  # about 0.64
print(chance_of_at_least_one_false_positive(0.05, 100)) # about 0.994

blocks.text: 4.2 Correcting for Multiple Comparisons

Standard corrections exist to keep the overall false positive rate under control when running many tests. The Bonferroni correction is the simplest: divide the target alpha by the number of tests, and require each individual p-value to clear that stricter, smaller threshold before being called significant. More refined methods, such as the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, control the expected proportion of false positives among all rejected tests rather than the chance of any single false positive, which tends to preserve more statistical power when many tests are run.

blocks.title: Pre-register the analysis plan
blocks.content: The most reliable defense against p-hacking is deciding, before looking at the data, exactly which metrics will be tested, how many tests will be run, and what correction will be applied. Deciding this after seeing preliminary results defeats the purpose entirely.

blocks.text: 5. Statistical Significance Versus Practical Importance

A tiny p-value only tells you that an effect is unlikely to be pure chance; it says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter. With a sufficiently large sample size, even a trivially small, practically meaningless difference can produce an extremely small p-value, because standard error shrinks as sample size grows, making the test statistic large even for a tiny true effect.

A classic example: testing 10 million users shows that a new button color increases click rate from 4.000 percent to 4.002 percent with a p-value of 0.0001. The result is statistically significant beyond any reasonable doubt, yet a 0.002 percentage point change is unlikely to be worth the engineering and design cost of shipping it. Statistical significance answers "is this probably real," while practical significance, usually measured by effect size, answers "is this big enough to matter."

items: Always report an effect size, such as a difference in means or a percentage point change, alongside any p-value.
A confidence interval on the effect size shows both whether the effect is likely nonzero and how large it plausibly is.
Set a minimum meaningful effect size before running the experiment, so a statistically significant but practically trivial result does not get shipped by accident.
Remember that with enough data, almost any null hypothesis of exact equality will eventually be rejected, since real world quantities are rarely exactly equal down to infinite precision.

blocks.text: A result can be statistically significant, a small p-value, while the actual size of the effect is too small to matter for any real decision, always ask how large the effect is, not just whether a p-value cleared the significance threshold.
6. Computing a P-Value with scipy.stats

In practice, p-values are computed with well tested statistical libraries rather than by hand. The scipy.stats module in Python provides ready made functions for the most common tests, each of which returns both a test statistic and its associated p-value directly.
Nearly every standard statistical test implemented in scipy.stats returns a p-value directly alongside its test statistic, sparing the need to manually look one up from a printed statistical table.
6.1 A Two-Sample T-Test Example

Comparing two groups of continuous measurements, such as conversion times or model latency, typically uses scipy.stats.ttest_ind, which runs an independent two-sample t-test and returns the p-value directly, saving the analyst from looking up critical values in a t-distribution table by hand.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

model_a_latency_ms = np.array([120, 115, 130, 128, 119, 122, 131, 117])
model_b_latency_ms = np.array([108, 112, 105, 110, 109, 111, 107, 106])

t_statistic, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(model_a_latency_ms, model_b_latency_ms)
print(f"t statistic: {t_statistic:.3f}, p-value: {p_value:.5f}")

alpha = 0.05
if p_value < alpha:
    print("Statistically significant difference in latency between models")
else:
    print("No statistically significant difference detected")

blocks.text: 6.2 A Proportion Test Example

Comparing two conversion rates or click-through rates, which are proportions rather than continuous measurements, typically uses a two-proportion z-test, available through statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportions_ztest, which is the appropriate tool for exactly the kind of A/B test dashboard metric most product and machine learning teams check daily.

code.content:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

# successes and totals for each of two groups
conversions = [412, 460]   # [old design, new design]
visitors = [5000, 5000]

z_statistic, p_value = proportions_ztest(conversions, visitors)
print(f"z statistic: {z_statistic:.3f}, p-value: {p_value:.5f}")

blocks.text: 7. Reading P-Values in AI and A/B Testing Dashboards

Most A/B testing dashboards used by product and machine learning teams display a p-value or a "statistical significance" indicator directly next to each metric. Reading these correctly, rather than treating a green checkmark as absolute proof, is a practical daily skill. A dashboard showing p equals 0.03 for a new ranking model means the observed lift would be unlikely under the assumption of no real difference, not that the new model is definitely better, and not that there is only a 3 percent chance the team is wrong.

This matters especially when many metrics are monitored simultaneously, which is the normal situation on a modern experimentation dashboard tracking clicks, conversions, latency, retention, and revenue all at once for the same experiment. Watching a dozen metrics for a single experiment and declaring victory the moment any one of them crosses p less than 0.05 is a direct instance of the multiple comparisons problem, and it is one of the most common ways teams fool themselves into shipping changes that provide no real benefit.

items: Decide the single primary success metric for an experiment before it launches, and treat other metrics as secondary or exploratory.
Apply a multiple comparisons correction, such as Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg, when genuinely testing many model variants or many metrics at once.
Avoid continuously monitoring a live experiment and stopping the instant a metric crosses significance, since repeated peeking is a subtle form of p-hacking.
Report the effect size and confidence interval next to any p-value from a model comparison, not the p-value alone.

blocks.title: A dashboard green checkmark is not a guarantee
blocks.content: Automated experimentation platforms often flag a metric as "significant" purely based on p less than 0.05. Treat this as one input to a decision, alongside effect size, business cost, and whether many other metrics were also being watched at the same time.

blocks.text: A dashboard reporting a p-value below the chosen threshold is signaling that the observed difference between two variants is unlikely to be pure chance, though it says nothing on its own about whether that difference is large enough to act on.
8. P-Values and Sample Size

A p-value depends heavily on sample size, given enough data, even a tiny, practically meaningless effect can produce a very small p-value, while a genuinely large effect measured on a very small sample can produce a large, non-significant p-value purely from lack of statistical power. This is precisely why section 5 stresses reporting effect size alongside the p-value, rather than the p-value alone.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np
small_effect = np.random.normal(0.001, 1, 100000)   # tiny true effect, huge sample
print(stats.ttest_1samp(small_effect, 0))   # can still produce a very small p-value

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A conversion rate difference of 0.01 percent between two webpage designs can register as statistically significant, a small p-value, once millions of visitors are included in the test, even though a difference that tiny is very unlikely to matter for the business.

blocks.text: This sample size sensitivity is a large part of why modern experimentation platforms increasingly report a confidence interval on the effect size alongside the p-value, giving a fuller picture than the p-value can provide alone.
9. Worked Example: Interpreting a P-Value Correctly

A team compares two versions of a search ranking model on click-through rate across 8,000 queries per version. The observed click-through rate is 12.4 percent for the current model and 13.1 percent for the new model. Running a two-proportion z-test in code produces a p-value of 0.021.

code.content:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

clicks = [992, 1048]     # [current model, new model], out of 8000 each
queries = [8000, 8000]

z_statistic, p_value = proportions_ztest(clicks, queries)
print(f"z statistic: {z_statistic:.3f}, p-value: {p_value:.4f}")
# z statistic: -2.307, p-value: 0.0211

blocks.text: The correct interpretation: if the new model truly performed no differently from the current one, a click-through rate gap this large or larger would appear in only about 2.1 percent of repeated experiments of this size, purely from sampling noise. Since 0.021 is less than alpha equals 0.05, the team rejects the null hypothesis and treats the new model as a statistically significant improvement.

The incorrect interpretation would be to say "there is a 97.9 percent chance the new model is really better" or "there is a 2.1 percent chance we are making a mistake by switching." Neither of those statements follows from the p-value itself. The team should also check the effect size, a 0.7 percentage point lift, against the cost of deploying the new model before deciding it is worth shipping.

Writing out the correct interpretation in full sentences, rather than just quoting the number, is a good habit for catching the misinterpretation trap from section 3 before it slips into a report or a team discussion.
10. Common Mistakes

items: Reporting the p-value as "the probability the null hypothesis is true," which reverses the actual conditional probability the p-value represents.
Treating a p-value just above 0.05, such as 0.06, as meaningfully different in strength of evidence from a p-value just below it, such as 0.04.
Running many simultaneous tests or metrics against one experiment and calling it a win the moment any single one clears p less than 0.05, without correcting for multiple comparisons.
Reporting a small p-value alone without an effect size, letting a large sample size make a practically meaningless difference look impressive.
Repeatedly checking an in-progress experiment and stopping it as soon as the p-value crosses the threshold, which is a hidden form of p-hacking.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: treating a p-value slightly above 0.05, like 0.06, as proof of no effect, a p-value just above the threshold is weak evidence against the null, not strong evidence for it.
11. Practice: Compute and Interpret a P-Value

A machine learning team wants to compare average user session length between two recommendation model versions, using session data collected from an A/B test. Complete the code below to compute the p-value with scipy.stats, then write one sentence stating the correct interpretation of the result, and one sentence stating a common incorrect interpretation to avoid.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

# session length in minutes for users under each model
session_length_control = np.array([...])
session_length_treatment = np.array([...])

# TODO: run an independent two-sample t-test and extract the p-value
t_statistic, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(session_length_treatment, session_length_control)

alpha = 0.05

# TODO: print the reject or fail to reject decision by comparing
# p_value to alpha, then compute and print the observed difference
# in means as an effect size alongside the decision
mean_difference = session_length_treatment.mean() - session_length_control.mean()

blocks.text: As a check: the correct interpretation names alpha, the observed p-value, and states the decision purely as "would a difference this large be unlikely under no real effect," while the incorrect interpretation to flag is any version of "there is a 95 percent chance the new model is better," which the p-value alone can never establish.
Write down the correct plain-language interpretation of the resulting p-value before comparing it against the incorrect interpretation from section 3, to check the distinction has genuinely sunk in.
Key Takeaway

Sample size dependence, covered in section 8, is a critical qualifier on everything else in this lesson, a p-value alone never tells the full story without also knowing how much data produced it and how large the underlying effect actually was.

A p-value measures how surprising the observed data would be if the null hypothesis were exactly true, nothing more. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it is not the probability that rejecting it would be a mistake, and treating it as either leads directly to overconfident conclusions and, at scale, to p-hacking when many tests are run against the same data.

Reading a p-value correctly, alongside a pre-chosen alpha, an honest count of how many comparisons were actually made, and a real effect size rather than the p-value in isolation, is what separates a trustworthy A/B test or model comparison from one that merely looks convincing on a dashboard.

Reading p-values correctly, alongside effect size, confidence intervals, and an honest accounting for multiple comparisons, is one of the most practically important statistical literacy skills for anyone interpreting experiment results in a data driven organization.
